lead: A level gives staff readings, not heights. The level book records each reading in its proper column, and reduction turns the readings into reduced levels. There are two standard methods. The height of collimation (HI) method finds the RL of the line of sight once per set-up and subtracts each reading from it. The rise and fall method compares each reading with the one before it from the same set-up. Both end with arithmetic checks that must be run on site, while a wrong page can still be re-read.
prereq: You need: backsight, intermediate sight, foresight and change point from Levelling terms, and the field patterns of Differential, fly and profile levelling.

sections.h3: The level book and the height of collimation method

blocks.text: Each line of the level book is one staff station. The columns are Station, BS, IS, FS, then either HI (height of collimation method) or Rise and Fall (rise and fall method), then RL and Remarks. A change point takes one line with its FS and its BS side by side, because both readings are on the same point. A staff held upside down against the underside of a beam, a bridge soffit or a ceiling is an inverted staff; its reading is booked with a minus sign, because the point is above the line of sight.

items: Write the BM and its RL. HI of set-up 1 = RL of BM + BS.
For every IS and the FS of that set-up: RL = HI − reading. An inverted reading −r gives RL = HI + r.
At a change point, the RL found from its FS plus the new BS gives the next HI: HI(new) = RL(CP) + BS(new).

blocks.text:
Check 1:  ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL
Check 2 (full):  Σ(each HI × number of IS and FS reduced from it) − ΣIS − ΣFS = sum of all RLs except the first
blocks.where: Check 1 tests only the BS, FS and change-point arithmetic. Check 2 also tests every intermediate subtraction; without it, a slip in an IS line passes unnoticed.

blocks.text: Within one set-up the line of sight is fixed, so a smaller reading means the staff stands on higher ground. Compare each reading with the previous reading from the same set-up (the previous reading of a change-point line is its BS, for the next comparison):
previous reading − present reading = + (a rise)  or  − (a fall);   RL = previous RL + rise, or previous RL − fall
blocks.where: Rise and fall are booked as positive numbers in their own columns; the heading carries the sign. An inverted reading is used with its minus sign, so 0.580 followed by −1.725 is a rise of 0.580 − (−1.725) = 2.305 m.

blocks.text: Check:  ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL
blocks.where: Every IS enters a rise or a fall, so this one three-way check tests all the arithmetic.

items: HI method: fewer calculations with many intermediate sights, so it suits profiles, contouring and setting out.
Rise and fall: more arithmetic, but one check covers every reading, so it suits fly and check levelling.
Neither check finds a misread staff: the level book balances with wrong readings. Only closing on a known benchmark does.
To complete a page with missing entries, use the column relations: rise or fall from two readings, a reading from a rise or fall, and a missing BS from the final RL and Check 1.

examples.question: The following readings were taken with a level and a 4 m staff on ground falling towards a stream crossed by a bridge: 1.235 (BM, RL 100.000 m), 1.870 (P1), 2.645 (P2), 3.410 and 0.580 (change point CP1), −1.725 (staff inverted under the bridge soffit S), 1.465 (P3, on the bank below S), 2.950 and 1.105 (change point CP2), 2.230 (P4), 2.865 (TBM). Book and reduce the levels by the height of collimation method and by the rise and fall method, apply all the checks, and find the clear height of the soffit above P3.
steps: Full HI check: Σ(HI × n) = 101.235 × 3 + 98.405 × 3 + 96.560 × 2 = 792.040; minus ΣIS (6.485, the inverted reading counted as −1.725) and ΣFS (9.225) gives 776.330 m, which equals the sum of the eight RLs after the BM, 776.330 m.
Clear height of soffit above P3 = 100.130 − 96.940 = 3.190 m (the fall from S to P3).
examples.answer: RLs: P1 99.365, P2 98.590, CP1 97.825, soffit 100.130, P3 96.940, CP2 95.455, P4 94.330, TBM 93.695 m. All checks give −6.305 m and the full HI check balances at 776.330 m. The soffit is 3.190 m above P3.

examples.question: Complete the following page of a level book (rise and fall method) and apply the check. Station 1: BS 2.215, RL 150.000 (BM). Station 2: IS 1.680. Station 3: BS 1.950, FS missing, fall 1.210. Station 4: IS missing, rise 0.640. Station 5: IS 0.775. Station 6: BS missing, FS 1.435. Station 7: FS 2.310, RL 148.390.
steps: Station 7: fall = 149.840 − 148.390 = 1.450 = 2.310 − BS(6), so the missing BS at station 6 = 0.860 m.
examples.answer: Missing entries: FS at 3 = 2.890, IS at 4 = 1.310, BS at 6 = 0.860; RLs 150.535, 149.325, 149.965, 150.500, 149.840 m; all three check values are −1.610 m.

traps: Booking the FS and BS of a change point on two lines. They are on the same point, so they share one line; two lines make the rise and fall comparison skip a step.
Comparing a reading with the FS of the previous set-up. After a change point, the next rise or fall is worked from the new BS.
Dropping the minus sign of an inverted staff. The soffit is above the line of sight, so its RL = HI + 1.725, not HI − 1.725.
Believing Check 1 proves the HI page. It ignores the intermediate sights; use the full HI check, or a slip in an IS line goes through.

quiz.q: Write the check for the rise and fall method.
quiz.a: ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL.

quiz.q: Why does the rise and fall method suit check levelling better than the HI method?
quiz.a: Every reading enters a rise or fall, so its single check tests all the arithmetic, while Check 1 of the HI method skips intermediate sights.

quiz.q: Readings from one set-up on a BM of RL 25.000 m: BS 1.600, IS 2.350, IS 0.940, FS 1.200. Reduce by rise and fall and check.
In the HI reduction of the first worked example, the RL of P2 was written as 98.950 m instead of 98.590 m (a subtraction slip). Which check finds it?
quiz.a: Check 1 still balances, because P2 is an intermediate sight. The full HI check finds it: Σ(HI × n) − ΣIS − ΣFS is still 776.330 m, but the RLs now add to 776.690 m, a difference of 0.360 m. (A misread staff reduced correctly would pass both checks.)

quiz.q: A level book gives ΣBS − ΣFS = −1.610 m but ΣRise − ΣFall = −1.540 m. Where would you look first?
quiz.a: The 0.070 m difference is a rise and fall arithmetic or booking slip, not a reading error: re-work the rises and falls (especially next to change points, where the wrong reading is often compared), then re-add the RLs.

beyond: Not for the exam. Digital levels and data collectors record each reading with its station code, reduce the run automatically by either method and flag a misclosure before the surveyor leaves the line. The raw readings are kept, so a corrected benchmark RL can be applied later without re-booking. Search for electronic field book, level run adjustment software and bar-code levelling.
